Trussville lies northeast of Birmingham, straddling the Jefferson County and St. Clair County line. About 35 square miles make up the city, at 709 feet of elevation, with ZIP code 35173. U.S. Route 11 cuts through town. Shoppers head to Colonial Promenade at Trussville on the west side or to the Tutwiler Farm centers along Highway 11 near the I-59 and I-459 interchange.

A parcel in this city can belong to either county, so ask whichever county office sends your tax bill for the exact balance.

The 2020 census counted 26,123 people in Trussville, and the latest estimate is 27,273. Every census since 1950 has shown growth.

Housing counts from 2020 show 9,173 households in 9,492 units, with 3.4 percent of units empty. Rentals stood vacant at a rate of 9.4 percent, and owner homes at 1.3 percent. The city grew by more than 500 percent from 1980 to 2010, which means most houses are fairly recent, with a smaller share of older ones mixed in.

In the 1930s the federal Resettlement Administration built a planned neighborhood here called the Cahaba Project. It earned a place on the National Register of Historic Places in 2006. The plan called for 243 single-family houses and 44 duplexes on half to three quarter acre lots around a green known as The Mall.

Most were one- and two-level four-square homes with brick or wood siding, pine floors and metal roofs. The government sold them to the residents after World War II.

Owning one of these houses, or one nearby, can affect both repairs and buyer interest. Ask the city or the National Park Service which rules cover exterior changes before you plan work. Buyers will expect an old house to need updating, and a seller who can describe the roof, wiring and plumbing history is in a stronger position when price comes up.

Trussville City Schools teaches 4,269 students. Until 2005 the schools belonged to Jefferson County Schools. They separated after a county financial crisis forced budget cuts that the city could not cover, and the city council had created its own Board of Education in 2004.

Five schools make up the system:

  • Hewitt-Trussville High School, grades 9 to 12
  • Hewitt-Trussville Middle School, grades 6 to 8
  • Cahaba Elementary School, grades K to 5
  • Magnolia Elementary School, grades K to 5
  • Paine Elementary School, grades K to 5

Families usually ask which elementary school an address feeds. Get the answer from the district office before you advertise.

Trussville draws families, and many of them hope to move in without doing work. A house that needs repairs can mean weeks of fix-ups, showings and waiting in a conventional listing. Selling directly for cash skips the repairs and any lender conditions. Set the offer next to what a repaired listing might bring once costs are subtracted, then choose.

The yearly property tax bill is due October 1 and becomes delinquent after December 31. Contact the Jefferson County or St. Clair County office that bills your parcel for the exact amount.

Alabama Code section 40-22-1 sets the recordation tax at 50 cents on each $500 of value, counting any fraction of $500. Value above a mortgage that already paid mortgage tax is what gets taxed. The proceeds divide two thirds to the state and one third to the county. Your closing agent will give you the final figure.

  • Start the title search early.
  • Expect liens and unpaid taxes to be paid at closing.
  • Bring proof of the purchase price to the recording office.

A loan on the house will not prevent a sale. Before closing, the title company obtains a payoff letter from your lender and the current tax figure from the county, and both are paid out of your proceeds. Liens found in the title search are cleared in the same step.

Unsure what is recorded against your property? Read the search before agreeing to a date. A lien you did not expect can shrink what you take home, and fixing it ahead of time is easier than fixing it at the table.

Cash makes sense when you would rather skip repairs and showings. Typical Trussville cases:

  • An older Cahaba Project house that needs updating.
  • An inherited house that relatives want sold quickly.
  • A rental with a tenant situation you want to end.
  • A house with deferred roof, plumbing or foundation work.

The sequence is simple. You describe the house and we respond with an offer. If you accept, a title company or attorney confirms ownership, arranges payoffs and agrees a closing day with you. Bring a photo ID, the deed or estate papers and, for a rental, the lease.

We buy Trussville houses as they are. You may request an offer and decide whether it fits.

Ask for any offer in writing and find out who pays closing costs. Check whether the sale depends on a loan, an appraisal or an inspection, since each of those can derail a deal late. Work out the net from each route, counting repairs, agent fees and the cost of carrying the house while it is listed.

Ask how fast the buyer can close and whether the date is firm. Read the contract in full, and have the closer explain anything unclear. Until you sign, you are free to walk away.

At closing you meet the closer, either in person or by mail with a notary, and sign the deed and the settlement statement. The deed is recorded, the recordation tax and recording fee are paid, any loan and tax balance are cleared, and the remainder comes to you.

Read the settlement statement line by line before you sign and ask about any charge you do not recognize. If someone is still living in the house, agree on a move-out date in writing. Hand over keys and garage openers at closing, then cancel or transfer utilities and forward your mail.

A cash buyer does not need a staged house, but a little order helps the offer. Clear out trash, turn the utilities on so the systems can be tested, and write down which appliances and fixtures stay. Be frank about leaks, cracks and old systems. A buyer who learns about them up front makes an offer that holds.

If the house came to you through an estate, the first step is showing who has the legal right to sign. Check with the probate office or an attorney, and gather the deed and the death certificate if you have them. A closing cannot proceed without that proof.

If a tenant lives in the house, share the lease and rent record with the buyer. Some buyers will close with a tenant still there, while others prefer an empty house, so say which you want at the start.

faqs.a: Jefferson and St. Clair counties, within the Birmingham metro area.

faqs.q: When did Trussville become a city?
faqs.a: It became a town on June 10, 1947, and a city on May 31, 1957.
A planned neighborhood of 243 single-family houses and 44 duplexes built in the 1930s by the federal Resettlement Administration. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2006.

faqs.q: Who runs the schools in Trussville?
faqs.a: Trussville City Schools, which split from the Jefferson County system in 2005 and teaches 4,269 students.

faqs.q: Do I need repairs before selling my Trussville house for cash?
faqs.a: No. We buy as is, so you can request an offer without fixing anything first.
